## Get the course workspace

Your VS Code course workspace holds your journals, notes, and project files in one Git-tracked folder. You do not download a ZIP: open the template on GitHub, click **Use this template** to create your own copy, then clone it into VS Code.

[Use the template on GitHub](https://github.com/AURA-Lab-SIUE/v2v-workspace){.btn .btn-primary .btn-lg}
[Setup guide](workspace-setup.qmd){.btn .btn-secondary}

**What's inside:** `00_inbox` (quick capture), `01_journal` (weekly reflections), `02_literature` (reading notes), `03_project` (prospectus, codebook, data, drafts), `04_resources` (attachments), and `_templates` (journal and codebook templates).

---

## Something broken?

Four problems have come up across the course. The **Fix It** page has each one in plain
steps: strange characters when you run a cell, a missing `Git: Clone` command, an install
that ends in "there is no package called v2v", and an install that will not finish when you need R
for class. For that last one, open your own workspace repository on github.com and click **Code**,
then **Codespaces**, then **Create codespace on main**: R, the course packages, and the R Companion
are already installed there.

[Fix It](fix-it.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}

## Check your setup

`00-check-your-setup.qmd` walks you through every install, one gray box at a time, and
tells you what each box should print. Save it into your workspace folder and open it in
VS Code. Run it whenever something stops working, not only in week one.

With the AURA Lab R Companion installed, run **Check my setup** from the Command Palette instead;
the file still works without it.

[Download 00-check-your-setup.qmd](../starters/00-check-your-setup.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}

## Commit your work to GitHub

`01-commit-your-work.qmd` walks you through saving, staging, committing, and pushing, with
what you should see at every step and what to do when it does not happen. Save it into the
**top folder** of your workspace, next to `README.md`.

Getting that file onto GitHub is itself the check: it is deliberately not in the workspace
template, so if it appears in your repository, you put it there.

[Download 01-commit-your-work.qmd](../starters/01-commit-your-work.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}

## Coding the codebook (Chapter 9)

`09-coding-the-codebook.qmd` walks you through creating your White Paper project, moving your
codebook into it, and taking a first look at the example data, with what each step should
print. Save it into the **top folder** of your workspace, next to `README.md`.

[Download 09-coding-the-codebook.qmd](../starters/09-coding-the-codebook.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}

## Wrangling the data (Chapter 11)

`11-wrangling-data.qmd` is the Data Wrangling worksheet, part 1 of the Twitch job: you hand-code
thirty messages, then import, diagnose, convert, join, and save one clean `.RDS` file. The routine
code is written for you, the core steps are blanks you fill, and each step says what it should
print. Save it into the **top folder** of your workspace, next to `README.md`. The
[Data Wrangling risks guide](risks/data-wrangling.qmd) shows the traps on this job.

[Download 11-wrangling-data.qmd](../starters/11-wrangling-data.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}

---

## Describing the data (Chapter 12)

The Describing Data worksheet is part 2 of the Twitch job. It loads the `twitch_analysis.RDS`
file you saved in part 1, with your thirty hand-coded messages inside, and walks you through
frequency tables, means and medians, a cross-tabulation, and three figures. The routine code is
written for you, the core steps are blanks you fill, and each step says what it should print.
Save it in the same folder as the Data Wrangling worksheet. Download the one for your course. The
[Describing Data risks guide](risks/describing-data.qmd) shows the traps on this job.

[Download the MC 451 worksheet](../starters/12-describing-data-mc451.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}
[Download the MC 501 worksheet](../starters/12-describing-data-mc501.qmd){.btn .btn-primary}

## Learning templates

Ready-to-use templates live in your course workspace under `_templates/`.

- **Weekly journal template** reflects on your learning using one of three thinking paths: the Connector (how does this relate to what I know?), the Troubleshooter (what problems did I solve?), and the Critic (does this match my experience?).
- **Data dictionary / codebook template** defines your variables in Phase III, with columns for variable name, definition, type, allowed values, and examples.

[Open the workspace](../workspace.qmd){.btn .btn-sm .btn-secondary}

## FAQ {#faq}

**Q: Do I need to buy the textbook?**
No. *From Vibes to Variables* is free and open access. [Read it online](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v/).

**Q: Can I use RStudio or another editor instead of VS Code?**
This course standardizes on VS Code so everyone shares one environment and one set of instructions. Learning it deeply is part of the course.

**Q: Do I need a separate note-taking app?**
No. Your notes live as Markdown files in the course workspace. Keeping everything in VS Code is the whole point.

**Q: Where do I turn in my work?**
Submit everything in Blackboard. Committing to GitHub is your backup, not your submission.

**Q: Can I work with classmates?**
You may talk through ideas with classmates, but your coding, analysis, and writing are your own. You are the only coder on your project.

**Q: What if I fall behind?**
Reach out to Dr. Leith early. The phases are structured but timelines can flex.

## Check your own work

Four pages built for this course. Each one runs in your browser: no account, no install, nothing
uploaded, and nothing you paste is seen by anyone. They check structure and arithmetic, they never
grade, and using one is not required.

- [Codebook Check](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/codebook-check/) reports what your codebook is missing
  against what the assignment asks for, including category pairs that may overlap.
- [Agreement Check](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/agreement-check/) takes two columns of codes and
  returns percent agreement, the reliability statistic, and the items the two passes split on. It
  handles one coder at two times, which is the stability this course asks for.
- Inside VS Code, the R Companion's **Reliability grid** does the same from two columns and writes the R
  code for your script.
- [Sampling Check](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/sampling-check/) turns your own coding rate into a
  corpus size, sizes the reliability subset, and reports the smallest effect that sample could find.
- [Inferential Check](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/inferential-check/) recomputes your chi-square or t
  test from your own numbers and gives you the APA sentence to check your write-up against.
- Inside VS Code, the Test group of the R Companion's **Write R code** runs the four tests in your script, and its
  **APA numbers to check your sentence** prints the numbers in APA form. Inferential Check stays a second
  opinion on the numbers.
